title: Team Building Basics - Roles, Type Coverage & Synergy
description: Learn how to build balanced, effective Pokémon teams in Polished Crystal. Understand team roles (sweepers, walls, support), type coverage strategies, offensive and defensive synergy, and common team archetypes. Build competitive teams that can handle any opponent.

Introduction

Building an effective Pokémon team means much more than just using your favorites. An effective team needs both offense and defense. This guide will help you understand the fundamentals of team building in the context of Polished Crystal.

Whether you're assembling a team for the main story, post-game content, or battling friends, these guidelines will help you build efficient teams.

Core Team Roles

Most successful teams use Pokémon with certain roles. Knowing these roles will help you build well-rounded teams:

Physical Sweeper

Purpose: Deal heavy physical damage and knock out opponents quickly.

Key Stats: High Attack and Speed

Example Pokémon:

  • Dragonite - Powerful Dragon/Flying with Outrage, Earthquake, and Extremespeed
  • Heracross - Bug/Fighting with Megahorn and Close Combat
  • Scizor - Bug/Steel with Bullet Punch and U-Turn

Typical Moves: STAB moves, coverage moves, priority moves

Special Sweeper

Purpose: Deal heavy special damage, often faster than Physical Sweepers.

Key Stats: High Special Attack and Speed

Example Pokémon:

  • Alakazam - Fast Psychic-type with Psychic and Shadow Ball
  • Espeon - Special attacker with Psychic and Signal Beam
  • Starmie - Water/Psychic with Hydro Pump and Psychic

Typical Moves: Special STAB moves, coverage moves like Thunderbolt/Ice Beam

Physical Wall

Purpose: Absorb physical hits and wear down opponents.

Key Stats: High Defense and HP

Example Pokémon:

  • Steelix - Steel/Ground with massive Defense
  • Skarmory - Steel/Flying with Spikes and Roost
  • Forretress - Bug/Steel that sets up hazards

Typical Moves: Recovery moves, status moves, entry hazards

Special Wall

Purpose: Tank special attacks and provide defensive utility.

Key Stats: High Special Defense and HP

Example Pokémon:

  • Blissey - Highest HP in the game with Soft-Boiled
  • Umbreon - Dark-type with Wish and Protect
  • Snorlax - Normal-type with Rest and Sleep Talk

Typical Moves: Recovery, status moves, support moves

Support/Utility

Purpose: Assist the team with status effects, healing, or field effects.

Key Stats: Varied - depends on role

Example Pokémon:

  • Clefable - Fairy with Wish and Heal Bell
  • Umbreon - Dark-type with Wish and Baton Pass
  • Forretress - Bug/Steel that sets hazards and uses Toxic

Typical Moves: Thunder Wave, Toxic, Wish, Heal Bell, Spikes

Lead/Setup

Purpose: Start battles strong, set up entry hazards, or gain early momentum.

Key Stats: Usually high Speed or bulk

Example Pokémon:

  • Aerodactyl - Fast lead with Rock Slide and Roar
  • Steelix - Bulky lead with Earthquake and Stone Edge
  • Jolteon - Fast special attacker with Thunderbolt and Hidden Power Ice

Typical Moves: Entry hazards, fast attacks, Roar to force switches

Type Coverage

Offensive Coverage

A good team should be able to hit all 18 types for at least neutral damage. This prevents being walled by specific Pokémon.

Example Core Coverage:

  • Fighting + Ghost - Covers nearly all types, but note that Ghost is immune to Normal and Fighting, and Normal is immune to Ghost
  • Ground + Ice + Fighting - Excellent neutral coverage across most types
  • Dragon + Ground + Fighting - Common offensive core with wide coverage

Coverage Moves to Consider

  • Earthquake - Hits Electric, Fire, Poison, Rock, Steel super effectively (immune: Flying, Levitate)
  • Ice Beam/Ice Punch - Hits Dragon, Flying, Grass, Ground super effectively (resisted by Fire, Water, Ice, Steel)
  • Thunderbolt - Hits Water, Flying super effectively (immune: Ground)
  • Fire Blast/Flamethrower - Hits Bug, Grass, Ice, Steel super effectively (resisted by Fire, Water, Rock, Dragon)
  • Shadow Ball - Hits Ghost, Psychic super effectively (immune: Normal; resisted by Dark, Steel)

Building Coverage

  1. Start with your sweepers - Choose their STAB moves first
  2. Identify gaps - What types can't your team hit effectively?
  3. Add coverage - Give Pokémon moves that cover weaknesses
  4. Account for immunities - Remember that some types are immune to certain moves (e.g., Ground vs Flying, Ghost vs Normal)
  5. Test your team - Make sure no type walls you completely

Defensive Balance

Resistances and Immunities

A balanced team should resist common attacking types and have immunities where possible.

Common Offensive Types to Resist:

  • Water - Very common, resisted by Water, Grass, Dragon
  • Fire - Common, resisted by Fire, Water, Rock, Dragon
  • Ice - Dangerous coverage, resisted by Fire, Water, Ice, Steel
  • Fighting - Powerful moves, resisted by Flying, Psychic, Fairy

Valuable Immunities:

  • Ground immunity - Flying, Levitate ability
  • Electric immunity - Ground-types
  • Fighting immunity - Ghost-types
  • Psychic immunity - Dark-types

Covering Team Weaknesses

If your Physical Sweeper is weak to Fire, make sure you have a teammate that resists or is immune to Fire. This allows safe switching.

Example:

  • Scizor is 4× weak to Fire
  • Partner with Starmie (resists Fire) or Arcanine (Fire-type, absorbs Fire moves with Flash Fire)
  • When Fire moves threaten, switch to your Fire resist

Defensive Synergy

Pair Pokémon that cover each other's weaknesses:

  • Dragon + Steel - Steel resists Dragon's weaknesses (Ice, Dragon, Fairy)
  • Water + Grass - Grass handles Water and Ground, Water handles Fire
  • Fighting + Ghost - Ghost is immune to Fighting's weakness

Team Synergy Examples

Example Core 1: Dragon/Steel (Offensive)

Core Pokémon:

  • Dragonite - Physical Sweeper with Outrage, Earthquake, Extremespeed
  • Scizor - Physical attacker with Bullet Punch, U-Turn, Superpower
  • Starmie - Special Sweeper with Hydro Pump, Psychic, Ice Beam

Why it works:

  • Excellent offensive type coverage
  • Dragonite and Scizor both have powerful physical moves and priority
  • Starmie provides special attacking pressure and rapid spin support
  • Steel-type resists Dragon and Ice (Dragonite's weaknesses)
  • Water covers Fire (Scizor's weakness)

Example Core 2: Balanced Wall + Sweeper

Core Pokémon:

  • Skarmory - Physical Wall with Spikes, Roost, Roar
  • Blissey - Special Wall with Soft-Boiled, Toxic, Seismic Toss
  • Heracross - Physical Sweeper with Megahorn, Close Combat, Stone Edge

Why it works:

  • Skarmory handles physical attackers
  • Blissey handles special attackers
  • Together they cover each other's weaknesses perfectly
  • Heracross provides offensive pressure while walls wear down opponents
  • Spikes from Skarmory makes Heracross's sweeps easier

Example Core 3: Weather-Based (Sun Team)

Core Pokémon:

  • Ninetales - Sets up Sunny Day, Fire moves boosted with Fire Blast
  • Venusaur - Grass/Poison benefits from sun (faster with Chlorophyll)
  • Arcanine - Fire-type with Extremespeed and boosted Fire moves

Why it works:

  • Sun boosts Fire moves and activates Chlorophyll
  • Venusaur becomes a fast sweeper under sun with Solar Beam (no charge time)
  • Fire attacks become devastating with sun boost
  • Water moves are weakened, protecting Fire-types

Common Mistakes

1. Too Many Sweepers

Problem: A team of 6 offensive Pokémon with no defensive backbone.

Why it fails: You'll get worn down quickly with no way to recover. One strong opponent can sweep your entire team.

Solution: Include at least 1-2 walls or defensive Pokémon for staying power.

2. Poor Type Coverage

Problem: Your team can't hit certain types effectively (e.g., all your Pokémon are walled by Steel-types).

Why it fails: Opponents will exploit your coverage gaps and wall you completely.

Solution: Ensure your team can hit all 18 types for at least neutral damage. Add coverage moves like Earthquake, Fire Blast, or Fighting moves to break through walls.

3. Overlapping Weaknesses

Problem: Multiple team members share the same weakness (e.g., 4 Pokémon weak to Ice).

Why it fails: One Ice-type opponent can threaten your entire team.

Solution: Diversify your team's types and ensure you have resistances to common attacking types. Use Pokémon with different type combinations to avoid stacking weaknesses.

4. No Pivot Pokémon

Problem: Your team has no Pokémon that can switch in safely and force switches.

Why it fails: You'll lose momentum and take unnecessary damage.

Solution: Include bulky Pokémon that can take hits and pivot out with U-Turn or Volt Switch (e.g., Scizor, Zapdos).

5. Ignoring Speed Tiers

Problem: Your entire team is slow with no priority moves.

Why it fails: Faster opponents will always move first and can pick you off before you attack.

Solution: Include fast Pokémon or priority move users (Quick Attack, Bullet Punch, Aqua Jet).

6. No Entry Hazard Control

Problem: You have no way to deal with Spikes or Toxic Spikes.

Why it fails: Hazards will wear your team down every time you switch.

Solution: Include a Rapid Spin user (e.g., Starmie, Forretress), or use Flying-types/Levitate ability to avoid Ground-based hazards.

Next Steps

Now that you understand team building basics:

  1. Build your first balanced team - Use the 6 roles as a template
  2. Test your team - Battle trainers and adjust as needed
  3. Experiment - Try different combinations and archetypes
